newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's embattled president denies he has quit.
newsitem.headline: Albania's embattled president denies he has quit.

text.p: President Sali Berisha, struggling against a breakdown in order in Albania after the collapse of shady investment schemes in January, denied rumours that he had resigned.
The official statement was issued late on Saturday after a show of force by police managed to curb random shootings in the capital, Tirana.
Berisha had faced growing demands for his resignation after armed rebels, many of whom had lost their life savings, seized control of a string of towns across the country.

Rumours earlier circulated in Tirana that he had quit. Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, speaking at a meeting of European Union ministers in the Netherlands, spoke of reports that he had resigned.
But the statement said Berisha intended to press on with an agreement signed with 10 political parties to hold early elections and repeated his pledge to step down if the parties backing him lost.
"Any attempt to deviate from this agreement will create division and have unforeseen consequences in deepening existing destabilisation," it said.
The Albanian government has responded to the crisis by asking for a foreign intervention force to restore order, but the response from Western powers was less than enthusiastic.
The United States said it was not ready to join a proposed stabilisation force in Albania, but appeared to leave the door open for that option later.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns also said all Americans who sought evacuation from Albania and were able to reach the U.S. embassy in Tirana had been airlifted out of the country.
He said the United States had evacuated 727 people from Albania since Thursday, including 319 on Saturday.
The Albanian government has mounted a sustained campaign, including the deployment of tanks and armoured personnel carriers on the streets of Tirana, to damp down lawlessness and armed insurrection.
The situation was notably calmer in the capital after the government improved the pay of police and sent them around town in armoured cars in a show of force.
But in the port of Durres, 30 km (20 miles) from Tirana, 5,000 Albanians broke through police lines in a desperate attempt to board a Greek frigate that had come to evacuate foreign diplomats.

Italy, Albania's biggest economic partner and a leading player in international efforts to halt the slide into chaos, suggested that Berisha's fate now lay in the hands of Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told the newspaper La Repubblica that Fino had to decide whether Berisha's presence was "an obstacle to pacifying the country or not, whether his continuation in the role can be accepted at least to prepare elections or not."
In the Dutch town of Apeldoorn, where EU foreign ministers discussed the crisis, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said Berisha should step down.

But Berisha said in the statement quoted by Albanian state television that he had no intention of resigning and would move forward with plans to hold elections under an all-party government appointed last week.
In Vienna, ambassadors of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) agreed to give broad support to the idea of sending troops to Albania to help to restore order.
The EU agreed to send a mission to Albania immediately to help in reconstruction efforts and to consider providing a small police force.
